summaries.example: Imagine the words “Mia runs and sings.” First, “runs” describes some people, and “sings” describes some people. When the two are joined with “and,” the meaning is the group of people who do both. If Mia is in that group, then Mia runs. This shows how the meanings of smaller parts help build the meaning of a whole sentence.
summaries.summary: Montague semantics is a way to study the meanings of natural language with the precision of mathematical logic. It was introduced by the logician Richard Montague and later developed by linguists, philosophers, and other logicians. Two central ideas are models and compositionality. A model gives rules for interpreting expressions in a possible situation. Compositionality says that the meaning of a larger expression depends on the meanings of its parts and on how grammar combines them. For example, the meaning of “walk and sing” can be built from the meanings of “walk” and “sing.” The approach also studies words such as “every,” sentences that can be understood in more than one way, and expressions whose truth changes from one possible world or time to another. Montague’s original system was highly explicit, but later work adapted it. Some researchers developed ways to handle questions, pronouns across sentences, and discourse. Others debated how strictly compositionality should guide a theory. Montague semantics is therefore both a particular historical theory and an important influence on modern formal semantics.
key_ideas: Montague semantics applies mathematical tools from logic to ordinary languages such as English.
It connects grammar, or syntax, with meaning, or semantics, in a systematic way.
A model describes how expressions are interpreted in a possible situation.
The meaning of a sentence can depend on possible worlds and times, not only on what is true here and now.
Later researchers changed and extended Montague’s ideas, including ways to study questions and connected conversations.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject shows how language can be studied with clear rules instead of only guesses about what sounds right. It helps explain why grammar and meaning are connected, why one sentence can have different readings, and how words such as “every” work. Its tools continue to influence the study of language and logic.

important_terms.definition: The study of what words and sentences mean.
The idea that a whole expression gets its meaning from its parts and how those parts are put together.
A carefully described possible situation used to check whether sentences are true or false. It is not necessarily the real world.
A sentence is true in every model. A sentence is a contradiction if it is true in no model.
A system that uses rules and symbols to describe how meanings fit together.

questions_to_think_about: Can a sentence have more than one meaning even when its words stay the same?
Why might a model be useful even if it is not a picture of the real world?
What meanings do the words in a sentence contribute?
Should every part of a sentence have a meaning of its own?

summaries.example: Consider “Every student read a book.” One reading allows different students to have read different books. Another can suggest that there is one particular book read by all the students. Montague-style theories explain such scope differences through the way noun phrases are interpreted and combined, sometimes using different derivations or later devices such as stored interpretations or discourse representations. The surface order alone does not always settle the meaning.
summaries.summary: Montague semantics is a mathematically explicit theory of natural-language meaning and its relation to syntax. Its central innovation was to bring model-theoretic methods, already familiar in formal logic, into the analysis of ordinary language. A model supplies interpretations for expressions relative to a formal space; it should not be identified simply with reality, since language ranges over hypothetical, imagined, and otherwise nonactual situations. The theory is organized by compositionality: each syntactic operation is paired with a semantic operation, so the interpretation of a complex expression is calculated from the interpretations of its constituents and their combination. This framework supports higher-order and intensional representations. An expression may denote a function, property, or relation, while a sentence may have an intension that varies over worlds and times. Lambda-abstraction provides a compact way to represent the contributions expressions make to larger structures. The framework explains quantifier phrases uniformly and helped produce generalized quantifier theory. It also addresses puzzles involving intensional verbs, such as the difference between finding and seeking a unicorn, and ambiguities of scope, as in “Every man loves a woman.” Montague’s original proposals were later revised. Discourse Representation Theory and dynamic approaches address connections across sentences; type-shifting and other syntactic theories modify the relation between categories and semantic types; pragmatics adds context and conversational factors. The entry presents compositionality as influential but contested, with several views about how strictly it should constrain semantic theory.
key_ideas: Montague treated natural-language semantics with methods associated with formal logic and gave an explicit account of a language fragment.
Compositionality links syntactic rules with semantic rules, though semanticists disagree about whether it is mandatory, merely useful, or an empirical ideal.
Models are not simply models of the actual world: they represent what language can describe, including hypothetical or impossible situations in the relevant formal space.
Intensional semantics represents meanings across possible worlds and times, helping analyze modality, attitudes, and verbs such as “seek.”
Scope ambiguity, anaphora, and discourse led to competing strategies, including quantifying-in, Cooper Stores, Discourse Representation Theory, and type-shifting or lifting rules.
Montague’s legacy includes generalized quantifiers, lambda-based representations, richer type systems, and continuing debates about syntax, pragmatics, and ontology.
summaries.why_it_matters: Montague semantics helped establish formal semantics as a field in which linguistic claims can be stated precisely and tested against models. It provides tools for analyzing quantifiers, ambiguity, modality, context dependence, and the relation between grammatical structure and meaning. Even theories that do not retain every original feature often develop ideas first made prominent in this tradition.

important_terms.definition: The study of meaning, especially the interpretation of linguistic expressions.
The claim that the meaning of a compound expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and their syntactic mode of combination.
A formal structure that assigns interpretations to expressions and is used to evaluate truth across possible situations.
The value of an expression when evaluated at a possible world and often a time; a sentence’s intension can be represented as a function to truth values.
The value an expression has at a particular world, time, and other relevant parameters, such as an individual or truth value.
A semantic system in which expressions can denote functions, properties, or relations of different logical levels, rather than only individuals.
An operation that represents a function by indicating what it does to an argument, as in a function that maps a property to whether it holds of an individual.
The interpretation of expressions such as “a,” “every,” and “most” as relations between sets or properties rather than as names of single objects.

questions_to_think_about: Does compositionality describe how people actually understand every sentence, or is it mainly a useful methodological standard?
Why can “John seeks a unicorn” fail to imply that unicorns exist, while “John finds a unicorn” normally does imply it?
Should logically equivalent tautologies always count as having the same meaning?
How should a semantic theory represent context-sensitive words such as “I,” “here,” and “this”?
Are higher-order entities in a semantic theory objects that language refers to, or convenient mathematical tools for describing composition?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “Every athlete trained with a coach.” This might mean that there was one coach who worked with every athlete, or that each athlete trained with possibly a different coach. The words themselves do not clearly tell us which person had the wider scope. A semantic theory must explain how these readings arise. Montague’s approach connects such differences to the way the sentence is derived and interpreted; later theories use tools such as stored noun-phrase meanings or discourse representations.
summaries.summary: Montague semantics is an approach to natural-language meaning developed from the work of the logician Richard Montague. It treats ordinary language as suitable for formal, mathematical analysis and connects syntax with semantics in a systematic way. Its main tool is model-theoretic semantics: a model assigns interpretations to expressions in a formally described possible situation. The point is not merely to copy the real world. Language can discuss the past, the future, possibilities, imaginary situations, and even situations that could not occur. A second central idea is compositionality. The meaning of a whole expression is calculated from the meanings of its meaningful parts and the grammatical rule that combines them. This makes it possible to explain why “John walks and sings” entails “John walks.” Montague’s system also uses higher-order logic and lambda-abstraction, which allow expressions to contribute properties, functions, and relations rather than only names of objects. Noun phrases such as “a pig,” “every pig,” and proper names can therefore receive a more uniform treatment. This led to generalized quantifier theory and analyses of expressions such as “no,” “most,” and negative-polarity items like “ever.” Intensional semantics represents an expression across possible worlds and times. It helps distinguish readings of “John seeks a unicorn,” since seeking need not imply that a unicorn exists, while finding one ordinarily does. The approach also studies scope ambiguity, pronoun reference, questions, and discourse. Later work changed some of Montague’s rules, introduced discourse representations and dynamic systems, and connected semantic interpretation with other grammatical theories. key_ideas: Montague semantics brought mathematical precision into the study of ordinary language.
Its theories connect syntactic rules with rules for calculating meaning.
A model is a formal possible situation, not necessarily a copy of the actual world.
Possible worlds and times help explain meanings involving possibility, necessity, wishes, and changing circumstances.
Quantifier phrases can create ambiguity about scope, or which phrase governs the interpretation of another.
Later researchers adapted the framework to questions, pronouns, discourse, context, and different views of grammar.
summaries.why_it_matters: Montague semantics matters because it shows that the meaning of ordinary sentences can be investigated with explicit rules and formal evidence. It helps explain ambiguity, quantifiers, possibility, context, and the connection between sentence structure and interpretation. Its methods influenced modern linguistics and philosophy of language, even when later researchers revised parts of the original theory.

important_terms.definition: The study of what words, phrases, and sentences mean.
The study of sentence structure and the rules for combining words.
A method that interprets language using formal models, which assign meanings in possible situations.
The principle that a complex expression gets its meaning from its parts and from the way grammar puts those parts together.
A meaning represented by how an expression would be interpreted across different possible worlds or times.
The particular thing, set, property, or truth value an expression picks out in a model.
A way to study words like “every,” “some,” and “most” by treating them as ways of relating properties or groups.
A symbol-based method for describing functions, including functions that take meanings as inputs.

questions_to_think_about: Why might “Every athlete trained with a coach” have more than one reasonable interpretation?
What can a formal model show that an example from the actual world cannot show?
Is it possible for a theory to explain idioms while still preserving compositionality?
Why might a sentence’s meaning need to include more than its truth value in the actual world?
When should a semantic theory use grammar alone, and when should it include context or conversation?
